about: Follow-up to the historical report post, answering the questions it raised: how is the tax bill set, and what raised it? The surprise: Prop 2 1/2 caps the town's total, not the bill, and everything voters approved -- overrides and debt exclusions -- is about a tenth of the average bill's rise since FY1991. Sends readers to /homes-and-taxes/growth-and-tax-rate, rebuilt as the destination.

text: Prop 2½ is usually described as a 2.5% cap on property taxes. It caps the town's total, not anyone's bill. Lunenburg's average single-family tax bill went from {g.facts[id=bill0].value.text} in {hr.first} to {g.facts[id=bill1].value.text} in {hr.base}, about {hr.bill_cagr}% a year. Grown 2.5% a year, it would be {g.facts[id=p25].value.text}.
So where did the rest come from? We split the rise using the state's own levy files:
• The 2.5% a year, compounding: {g.facts[id=s-cap].value.text} of the rise. It needs no vote.
• New growth: {g.facts[id=s-growth].value.text}. New homes and additions don't raise anyone else's bill, but they raise the average: our reading is that newer and bigger homes join it.
• Overrides and debt exclusions, everything voters approved: {g.facts[id=s-votes].value.text}.
• Homes carrying more of the total as businesses became a smaller share ({g.facts[id=rs0].value.text} of the levy, now {g.facts[id=rs].value.text}): {g.facts[id=s-homes].value.text}.
So if Lunenburg's taxes feel high, overrides and exclusions are about a tenth of the story.

The page also shows what does and doesn't change a bill: why a new business doesn't lower anyone's taxes, why a business closing raises them, and why the average bill rose {hr.dip.bill}% from {hr.dip.fy0} to {hr.dip.fy1} while home values fell {hr.dip.value}%.

These are averages from the state's Division of Local Services, and the split is our arithmetic on them. One home's bill moves with its own value; the average also moves when new and enlarged homes join it.
What did you think Prop 2½ capped? Tell us in the comments.
